title: What is the role of data and facts?
label: Role of data / and facts
question: How do we move beyond data, facts and archival absences while also framing the data and facts we have carefully, for what they tell (and don’t tell) us? How do we use current and past health statistics without being extractive?
more: Limitation named: People working in policy and advocacy are often trained to work in data-driven ways, even more than academics. How do we forge conversations that go beyond data, or reframe what data means in the first place?
source: Research agenda board, Critical health humanities column; discussed at length in the afternoon

title: Keeping Endarkened Co-Composition ethical as it travels
label: Keeping it ethical / as it travels
question: If Endarkened Co-Composition becomes a method others use, how do we tell meaningful collaboration from tokenistic engagement, and guard against extractive uses that cut against its ethical aims?
more:
Ideas from the room: Require reflection on critical positionality; articulate the lineage clearly (Toliver, after Dillard); insist on the full name rather than shorthand.
Also feeds: The critical position paper
source: Position paper board (EJW, CYL) and afternoon discussion (Lucy Green on how loosely ‘co-production’ is used)

title: What is the audience’s role in Endarkened Co-Composition?
label: The audience’s / role
question: If the aim is that fewer Black people die in hospitals, what is the audience’s part in the method? How do audiences respond, contribute to the sound, or act?
more:
Raised by: Lucy Green’s questions on how people respond; Gre named it as underdeveloped in the thesis; Lucy Lowe asked who the audience is, where and when, and why bend Endarkened Co-Composition toward one that “fetishises stats”; position paper board asked whether audiences sing along.
Ideas from the room: Clinicians and policymakers in the audience; audience contributing to the sound; staging in hospitals; creative responses that don’t feel like a feedback form.
source: Afternoon discussion; position paper board

title: Endarkened Co-Composition and fugitive anthropology
label: Fugitive / anthropology
question: How can we understand endarkened listening, co-presence and storytelling within the framework of fugitive anthropology?
source: Research agenda board, Anthropology and migration health column (methodological/conceptual question)

title: Time, depth and trust
label: Time / and trust
question: Anthropologists spend time building relationships and trust. Will this happen with Endarkened Co-Composition, and how? How would participants experience Endarkened Co-Composition as different from an NHS focus group?
more: From the discussion: Gre: Endarkened Co-Composition was never meant to be quick. It replaces solitary composition with a protocol, and even three days in Alabama made Deborah Mouton’s workshop possible. Existing practice: groups of no more than seven, full transcripts returned before text is set, participant input on the sound.
source: Position paper board (LL) and afternoon discussion

title: How does the demand for a clear account shape what patients say?
label: The demand for / a clear account
question: How do patients describe moments in gynaecological care when the demand for a clear, legible account changed what they felt able to say or what was noted by clinicians?
ec_adds: It treats what clinical settings usually discard as noise (hesitation, silence, what goes unsaid) as data. Patients compose their own account on their own terms; the researcher co-composes with them rather than extracting from them.
on_paper: NHS research ethics plus university ethics, with a trauma-informed protocol and consent that can be revisited and withdrawn. A pilot-scale methodology-development study with PPI from the start. For evidence, pair Endarkened Co-Composition with a familiar analysis of consultation notes.
with_whom: Gynaecologists, GPs, nurses and midwives; patients and community organisations led by Black women; medical humanities and anthropology colleagues; a clinical academic to hold NHS sponsorship; a sound practitioner trained in Endarkened Co-Composition.
risks: Extraction, re-harm, clinician defensiveness, recording consent and confidentiality, tokenising community partners, reviewers reading the work as “not evidence”.
note: Gre’s worked example on the board template, offered to be corrected.
source: Research agenda board, How to use this board

title: Trust when technology gets it wrong
label: Trust when technology / gets it wrong
question: Does Endarkened Co-Composition create trust, shared understanding, agency and space for forms of knowledge that technology alone cannot provide? If technology is imperfect, can Endarkened Co-Composition create a space where mistakes become opportunities for dialogue and collective learning rather than problems to be corrected?
risks: Collaboration can reproduce power inequalities, create pressure to participate, or give an impression of shared ownership when some still hold more control. How do we make sure trust in human relationships does not become uncritical trust in health systems?
more: Sub-questions: What happens when technology makes mistakes? Can human relationships help participants negotiate uncertainty, challenge technological decisions and keep creative ownership?
source: Research agenda board, Critical health humanities column

title: Birthing people, sound and agency
label: Birthing people, / sound and agency
question: How do birthing people create sound, and harness existing sound, to navigate medicalised and institutionalised spaces in a way that is healthy?
ec_adds: Confidence as a creator and curator of sound, from co-creating with others.
on_paper: NHS and university ethics. A pilot-scale methodology-development study with PPI from the start. Evidence: testimonies from birthing people and partners; clinicians’ notes.
risks: Clinician defensiveness; a birthing person afraid to take this leadership role in a medicalised space, in moments of vulnerability.
source: Research agenda board, Critical health humanities column

title: Better birthing spaces (very blue sky, or not)
label: Better birthing / spaces
question: How can sound, design, art and haptics make birth better in birthing centres, hospitals and homes? Or, how can asking about these things improve experiences?
where: Medical spaces, but also mobile (home births with midwives)
ec_adds: Birthing people already use strategies, and some purpose-designed birthing centres engage these issues, but medicalised spaces dominate. Could a checklist be a useful tool?
risks: Not yet drafted (“ran out of time, but there are many”).
note: In discussion, Christina offered the checklist as a way to make the idea feasible.
source: Research agenda board, Critical health humanities column

title: How temporalities in migrant communities’ everyday lives shape maternity care
label: Trust, time and / migrant maternity care
question: How can practitioners (midwives, GPs, obstetricians) build trust with patients from migrant communities and understand their priorities for maternity and newborn health services?
where: GP surgeries, maternity settings, community groups, migrant communities
ec_adds: Understanding opacity in people’s experiences: which lived experiences people share or don’t, and the tools they use to share them, as they navigate structures of migration and racism.
with_whom: Academic clinicians, community organisations, migrant communities
risks: Hierarchies of knowledge (biomedical rationalisations), extraction and re-harm
more: From the discussion: Mistrust is framed around migration status but may be structural: “I don’t think people die because they can’t speak English.” The challenge is to give policymakers something that makes sense, to do more than count.
note: Posted in both the Clinical and the Anthropology and migration health columns. It sits between the clinic and the community.
source: Research agenda board; Mary’s summary in the agenda discussion

title: Endarkened Co-Composition inside the medical research cycle
label: Inside the / research cycle
question: How can an Endarkened Co-Composition encounter be positioned within the numbers-heavy medical research cycle so that it creates the bravest and most honest space in which patient and public involvement and engagement (PPIE) can happen, even with all the numbers and measures?
more:
Precedent: Lucy Green’s arts-based workshops on pregnancy journeys with Black and South Asian women (with the Maternity Disparities Consortium), the Art of Creation exhibition and the British Science Festival activity.
Her own tension: Whether she can resist the urge to analyse and interpret without fearing that important data is lost.
source: Lucy Green’s provocation

title: Fostering cross-disciplinary conversation
label: Cross-disciplinary / conversation
question: How can Endarkened Co-Composition support conversations between clinical and medical researchers and creative, anthropological and humanities researchers?
ec_adds: With some glowing exceptions, medical humanities and creative approaches to medicine are often additive, and health scientists can move quickly to define what “the arts” mean. Endarkened Co-Composition strategies (workshops, conversations) may foster richer conversations among academics. Engaging communities matters, but so does cross-disciplinary curiosity.
risks: Becoming too navel-gazing; the tension between exploratory work, limited resources and urgent needs.
note: The symposium itself was a first test of this question.
source: Research agenda board, Other or cross-disciplinary column

title: Moral injury and the people who stay
label: Moral injury and / the people who stay
question: Can Endarkened Co-Composition-informed practice help clinicians facing burnout and moral injury, who know the problem without the means to fix it? Does that support retention?
more: From the discussion: Christina: time managed to the minute and the measurables that crowd out the caring work people came for. Catherine: arts engagement and wellbeing research; funders already pay to prevent burnout because training clinicians is expensive.
note: Worded from the transcript. Christina and Catherine to confirm.
source: Agenda discussion

title: Endarkened Co-Composition in training for future and new clinicians
label: Clinician / training
question: Can Endarkened Co-Composition carry Black people’s maternal experiences into arts-and-humanities-based training for future and new clinicians that emphasises belief in, and trust of, birthing people’s accounts of their bodies?
where: A university with community organisation partners
ec_adds: A perspective that challenges accepted knowledge and ways of doing and knowing. It acknowledges the discomfort but avoids the defensiveness that shuts down openness. Presented as a supplement to clinical and lab-based work focused on data.
on_paper: To be supported it needs to speak to the acknowledged gaps in outcomes that the science alone cannot explain.
more: From the discussion: Reach people early, before ways of knowing set. A “yes, and” approach: our usual ways of knowing have not solved this, so what else could we do? What does it mean to listen openly?
source: Research agenda board, Critical health humanities column

title: Loss as knowledge in the next pregnancy
label: Loss as knowledge in / the next pregnancy
question: How can the experiences of people who had negative maternity, perinatal or newborn care, including bereavement, reshape preconception and inter-pregnancy care, with that experience heard as knowledge and not only as trauma?
more: Context: Mary’s new, very preliminary preconception-blueprint work with Population Sciences. Many people with very negative birth experiences decide not to have more children. Bereaved families who return for another pregnancy risk having their loss read as anger rather than as knowledge of how services failed.
note: Worded from the transcript. Mary to confirm.
source: Mary’s introduction and the tension discussion

title: Story, numbers and policy
label: Story, numbers / and policy
question: What happens when statistics reach clinicians and policymakers alongside people telling their own stories in sound, untranslated and undistilled?
more: From the discussion: Catherine: in Nebraska, individual stories are what move policymakers, and advocacy groups now run storytelling trainings. Mary: measurement put maternal disparity on the table but risks turning it into “a marketing campaign”. Gre: numbers presented alongside self-told story, with sound as the vehicle, could be more impactful than “2.5 times”.
note: Worded from the transcript. Contributors to confirm.
source: Agenda discussion of the knowledge-hierarchies tension

title: Methodologies beyond a ‘deficit model’
label: Beyond the / deficit model
question: There is much talk of increasing access to healthcare and less about access to what. Rather than increasing access to inequitable practices, could access be reframed as a way to listen across, so that power doesn’t flow one way, in advocacy and policy? Could co-composition resist a colonialist deficit model of gynaecological knowledge and reproductive health by hearing alternatives?
more: Background: Music education and social justice scholarship that goes beyond the deficit model, recognising that communities already have their own musical traditions and knowledge.
source: Research agenda board, Community practice and advocacy column

title: Memory recollection as a collaborative practice: making sense of stories of health
label: Memory recollection as / collaborative practice
question: What role do composers and actors play in the co-creation process of recalling history, or the story of a moment in the past?
where: An informal community setting, a place of comfort (a living room)
ec_adds: It speaks directly to co-presence and agency, and to the relational work of deciding which memory is most ‘representational’ and creating an account of history.
with_whom: A multidisciplinary presence of social scientists and humanists to engage how a story forms, particularly the nuances of collective memory.
risks: Mostly at publication: crediting all contributors as equal participants.
note: Sits between community and archive. While writing, Chisomo said she was still working out when she might need to step back.
source: Research agenda board, Arts-based and creative practice column

title: Africa in the story of Black maternal death
label: Africa in the story of / Black maternal death
question: How can African and diasporic traditions of listening and storytelling, shared yet distinct, reconnect African maternal health to conversations about Black maternal death without collapsing their differences?
more: From the provocation: Africa has been filed under “development” and taken out of the equation of Black maternal death, although African women are also disproportionately affected. Chisomo called for locating the disruptions and connectivities for what they are.
note: Worded from the transcript. Chisomo to confirm.
source: Chisomo Kalinga’s provocation

title: After “cured”: Anarcha’s life
label: After / “cured”
question: What was Anarcha’s life like after she was labelled “cured”? Where did she go?
more:
How Endarkened Co-Composition works here: Speculation as a formal way of making knowledge in Black storytelling tradition. At the Alabama retreat, every team member independently placed Anarcha’s leaving of the hospital in winter, in snow, with her breath visible.
Output: The first lane of the opera
source: Gre’s opening framing and afternoon discussion

title: Knowledge hierarchies and measurement
label: Knowledge hierarchies / and measurement
question: Sides: clinicians and policymakers; us in the room and bereaved families; the legal sector. Listening to the whole narrative means trauma is also knowledge. In the US, story and lived experience do affect policymaking (CM).
source: Research agenda board, Tensions and gaps

title: Trust in people vs uncritical trust in systems
label: Trust in people vs / trust in systems
question: How do we ensure trust in human relationships does not lead to uncritical trust in health systems?
source: Research agenda board (CYL)

title: Science’s explanations, with or without race and gender
label: Science with or without / race and gender
question: Science’s explanations with and without contextualisation of race and gender. Catherine: “the science doesn’t explain why we have these problems. The problem is racism.”
source: Research agenda board, Tensions and gaps

title: The arts as an add-on vs the arts as method
label: Arts as add-on / vs method
question: The arts are often brought in additively, through medical humanities. Can it be more equitable to use the arts as a method of research?
source: Research agenda board, Tensions and gaps

title: Moral injury
label: Moral / injury
question: We know the problem but don’t know how to address it. Arts engagement offers wellbeing and a reason to stay.
source: Research agenda board, Tensions and gaps

title: “Good science” vs “wokeness”
label: “Good science” / vs “wokeness”
question: How do we keep it looking like good science and not “wokeness”? It may be inevitable. Yet and still, people are dying. Name the eugenic logic.
source: Research agenda board, Tensions and gaps; agenda discussion

title: Ethnographic time vs project time
label: Ethnographic time / vs project time
question: Years of relationship vs funded windows. The opera is planned over five to six years; partners hoped for 2027.
source: Afternoon discussion

title: Opacity vs translation as access
label: Opacity vs / translation as access
question: Refusing translation protects, but translation can be inclusion (sign interpretation, for example) or a route into care. Consultation and consent decide which.
source: Position paper board (CB)

title: Why centre clinical research?
label: Why centre / clinical research?
question: Clinical research is embedded in much of what Endarkened Co-Composition is trying to move away from. Who is this for, when, where and why?
source: Afternoon discussion (Lucy Lowe)

title: Dilution and tokenism
label: Dilution and / tokenism
question: Co-production is used lightly in medicine. Does partial adoption inch people forward, or dilute the method?
source: Position paper board; afternoon discussion

title: When music isn’t welcome
label: When music isn’t / welcome (NICU)
question: In Chi Ying’s neonatal intensive care project, students reshape the ward’s soundscape, including a pumping song requested by mothers. There are also times music is not wanted. Is there a place for music at all?
source: Chi Ying’s introduction

title: Sound theory as rigour
label: Sound theory / as rigour
question: Gre’s response to the “good science” worry: back up Endarkened Co-Composition’s claims with sound theory that treats sound as world-building and political, so its rigour is visible on its own terms.
source: Agenda discussion

title: Opera to keep doctors in Omaha
label: Opera to keep / doctors in Omaha
question: Twenty-odd years ago, funding Omaha’s opera was argued partly as a way to attract and keep medical professionals. The opera audience may include the people the message most needs to reach.
source: Afternoon opera discussion

title: “Hard to reach”, or choosing not to be reached
label: “Hard to reach”, / or choosing not to be
question: Princess Banda’s thesis examines the label “hard to reach”: why people may make themselves unreachable, because of failures to listen and distrust of medical institutions.
source: Lucy Lowe’s provocation

title: Home key and the sound of hesitation
label: Home key and / the sound of hesitation
question: Gre sets a piece’s key from the general home key of the interviewees’ speaking voices, and leaves ums and hesitations in: “the sound of hesitation is different than someone alluding to hesitation.”
source: Afternoon discussion

title: Voice and silence in incarcerated spaces
label: Voice and silence in / incarcerated spaces
question: Christina is preparing a first creative workshop through a prison-education collective. She sees Endarkened Co-Composition’s ideas of voice and opacity as useful for working with the silences of those settings.
note: Christina said this is deliberately not part of her research, as an ethic of the collective. Listed as a resonance, not a proposed site.
source: Christina’s introduction

title: “A drizzle of medical authority”
label: “A drizzle of / medical authority”
question: Proposed in the room as the title of something to write: a constant, fine, everywhere presence in the Scottish sense of drizzle. Gre hopes to find a middle ground between Scottish drizzle and cake drizzle.
source: Responses after the cosmogram walk (speaker to confirm)

title: “Nothing is True”
label: “Nothing / is True”
question: Medical students taking anthropology named a WhatsApp group “Nothing is True”. They are used to learning facts, and the course asks them to think differently.
source: Responses after the cosmogram walk

title: The cosmogram walk in the classroom
label: The cosmogram walk / in the classroom
question: Michelle wondered how she might use the walk with her students, who are interested in embodiment, while noticing her own urge to make it useful.
source: Responses after the cosmogram walk

title: Ultrasound: sound we can’t hear
label: Ultrasound: sound / we can’t hear
question: Obstetric ultrasound, developed in Glasgow, uses sound we cannot hear and made the foetus visible as a separate person. On Glasgow’s obstetric-led red pathway, size predictions were racialised and sometimes wrong, and drove coercive interventions.
source: Lucy Lowe’s provocation

title: Glass bangles and the womb’s soundscape
label: Glass bangles and / the womb’s soundscape
question: A workshop participant brought glass bangles from a traditional baby shower, whose sound reaches the baby in the womb. Lucy Green connected this to cultural traditions of care and to the physiology of foetal hearing, and played a recording of the womb.
source: Lucy Green’s provocation

title: Opera has always been modular
label: Opera has always / been modular
question: Piano reductions, sing-it-yourself versions and storybooks: opera has always travelled. A touring version with talkbacks, community and university spaces, and the audience singing along.
source: Afternoon opera discussion

title: The colonial archive of caesarean birth
label: The colonial archive / of caesarean birth
question: Erin’s research found British travel writers recasting caesarean section as a white technology, though successful caesareans had long been performed in Southern Africa, while more white women in Europe were dying of surgical births.
source: Erin’s introduction
